card st-build-card  [decided]
Every build opens a card obligation, and the pass closes it with a card or with the cards it followed
why: The obligation is data in the log, so a pass that changes code and leaves the map untouched shows as an open obligation. A pass that made no new decision closes it by naming the cards its choices came from, so it never writes a card only to meet a quota.
subtree: 2 cards, 2 decided

The CLI command that starts a build appends the obligation to the log, before any code is written.

When the pass writes a card, the agent places it: the title, the why, the parent in the refines tree, the depends_on. The CLI cannot choose the parent, because knowing what a decision refines is judgment. So the pipeline creates the demand and the agent satisfies it.

Nothing here can drift, because the obligation is data in the log rather than a line in a prompt. The open ticket shows what its builds proposed or followed (#vi-board-ticket-decisions-2). No card in the map shows an obligation.

A pass closes the obligation in one of two ways. It proposes one card for each decision that no card gives: a pass that makes three decisions writes three. Or, when every choice in its diff came from a cited card or from a card its search found, it records "no new decision" and names those cards. The grader checks that record against the diff the same way it checks the cited cards. A choice in the diff that none of the named cards gives fails the pass as an unrecorded decision. A list of values, a configuration, or the inside of one helper is not a decision, so it is never a reason to write a card.

Example:

- Card A "Each agent carries its role outside the prompt".
- Ticket T "Show the role in the launch record", which cites A.
- Pass P builds T.

1. The build starts. The log gets obligation O for P, and O is open.
2. P adds the role to the launch record. Every choice comes from A. P records "no new decision" and names A. O closes.
3. The grader reads the diff. Each choice traces to A, so the pass goes on.
4. P also picks a new file format that A does not give, and names only A. The grader fails the pass as an unrecorded decision. The next pass proposes a card for the format, and that card closes O.
5. P exits with neither a card nor a record. O stays open, and the ticket shows "No new card".

```
build starts ──> obligation O (open)
                      │
pass P ──┬── a decision no card gives ──> proposes card C ──> O closed by C
         └── every choice from cards ──> "no new decision: A" ──> O closed
                                               │
                       grader: a choice in the diff that A does not give ──> pass fails

O = the card obligation of one build   A = a card the pass names   C = a card the pass proposes
```

**1. The 600-second pass limit**
1. Kill on silence, not on total time. Use "no tool event for N minutes". A session that makes progress then runs to the end. This is my recommendation.
2. Raise the cap to about 20 minutes. It is cheap, but it hides a stuck session for longer.
3. Resume the killed session, not a fresh pass. The first pass in these builds had already spent about $1 to $2 of work, and a restart loses it.

Check first: the `pass-1.jsonl` files of the 7 killed builds. If the last event is a long `make test` or `make e2e` run, the cause is shared CPU load, not a slow agent. Then lower the number of parallel builds, not the limit.

**2. Merge conflicts**
1. Rebase the branch on the main line before the first check, and again right before the merge. A conflict then shows up before the build spends $3. This is my recommendation.
2. Give the agent the conflict. On a conflict, start a short pass that gets the conflict text and resolves it. Do not redo the whole ticket. The cost drops from about $3 to under $1.
3. Do not start two builds that name the same module at once. The build scheduler reads the files each ticket cites and serializes overlaps. This follows #werk-stack-modules.

Check first: which files conflicted. If it is always the same two or three files (`cli.ts`, `server.ts`, the card log), the real fix is to split those files, not to change the pipeline.

**3. Flaky merge checks**
1. Re-run a failed check once on the merge, before it counts as red. If the second run passes, record "flaky" with the test name in the log. This is cheap and measures the problem. This is my recommendation.
2. Fix the three tests: the log-appears test (3 s under load), the e2e navigation test, and the `heading` visibility test. Wait on a condition, not on a fixed time. This follows #werk-test-runner-parallel on load-aware limits.
3. Run the merge check with a lower worker count than the build check, so it does not compete with other builds.

A flaky failure that costs a full rebuild is the most expensive of the three. Option 1 for issue 3 pays back first.

card st-build-parallel  [decided]
Up to 3 unblocked tickets build at once, and two tickets build at the same time only when they touch no module in common
why: Ticket blocking edges give the order, and the modules each ticket touches give the overlap. Two tickets that edit the same module and build at the same time conflict at the merge queue.
subtree: 2 cards, 1 open, 1 decided

A ticket can start when every ticket in its blocked_by list is merged and no failed set check holds it (#st-ticket-partial). The run builds up to 3 such tickets at the same time, each in its own worktree.

**Overlap blocks.** Each ticket names the modules it changes, by name and not by file path (#st-ticket). The scheduler starts a ticket next to the ones already building only when its modules and theirs share none. A ticket that shares a module waits until the other ticket has merged, then builds on top of it. The comparison is of the names alone: no agent judges overlap.

**A conflict can still happen.** A list of modules can miss one. Then the second ticket fails its merge, and the merge queue sends it back to the builder (#st-build-conflict).

**The base.** Each worktree branches off the main line's tip at the moment its build starts. A ticket that starts after an earlier merge has that merge in its tree.

**The cap.** 3 is a first guess. It changes when a real machine or a real rate limit shows a better number. The merge queue still takes one ticket at a time.

card st-build-conflict  [decided]
A merge conflict rebuilds the ticket on the main line's tip and does not count against its retry cap
why: A conflict means another ticket merged first, not that this ticket is wrong. Counting it lets other tickets' merges use up this ticket's passes.

When a ticket's merge fails because git cannot merge it, the next build of that ticket starts fresh from the main line's tip, not from the ticket's old branch. The builder gets the conflict output as its last failure. That pass does not count against the retry cap (#st-build-run-mechanics).

A red check on the merged tree is still the ticket's own failure and still counts.

A ticket whose merge conflicts ten times in a row stops the merge loop as stuck, so a conflict that never resolves cannot run without end. The limit is high because up to three tickets build at once. A ticket that adds a line to a file that most tickets change, such as the list of commands, can lose the race to the main line several times before it merges.

A merge conflict is resolved on the ticket's own branch, and that ticket merges next
why: A fresh build takes as long as the first one. The main line moves again in that time, so a ticket that touches a busy file conflicts again and again.

When git cannot merge a ticket, the next pass starts from the ticket's own branch with the main line's tip merged into it. The builder gets the conflicted files and the conflict output, resolves them, and runs the checks. This replaces the fresh rebuild that #st-build-conflict sets. The pass still does not count against the retry cap.

A ticket that comes back green from a conflict pass goes to the front of the merge queue, so no other merge can move the main line under it first.

card lp-overseer-progress  [decided]
A classifier agent decides every 5 minutes whether the agent is looping
why: Progress has no fingerprint a program can compute: a loop that changes one character each pass looks new to any hash. Whether work moves forward is a judgement.

Every 5 minutes, the overseer starts a classifier agent for each running agent (#lp-overseer-det). The classifier has one task: say whether the agent is looping.

1. **Input.** The ticket's brief, and the tool calls since the classifier's last verdict. Not the whole log: it grows without limit, and old passes add noise.
2. **Output.** "looping" or "not looping", with a reason in one or two sentences.
3. **The wait.** The overseer waits for the verdict with a timeout, like any other tool call. No verdict counts as "not looping". The 60-second rules still apply to the agent (#lp-overseer-silence, #lp-overseer-inflight).
4. **On "looping".** The overseer cancels the agent and starts a fresh pass. The classifier's reason goes into the new pass's brief, so the next pass knows what did not work (#lp-stateless).

A loop can run for up to 5 minutes before a verdict. That is acceptable for a repeat. A hard stall is caught at 60 seconds by the other rules.

The cost is one model call per running agent every 5 minutes.

card lp-overseer-mechanics  [decided]
The overseer runs inside the headless runner; no verdict means deny or not looping
why: A timer beside the session it watches needs no second process. A classifier that does not answer must not widen a permission.

- The silence watchdog is a timer inside runHeadless, not a separate process.
- In-flight check: only the CPU time of the agent's child processes is read, with ps. A frozen call with no process of its own cancels the session, the same as silence. Output bytes, open files and connections are not read yet.
- Asks: only builder sessions send asks to the classifier. No verdict means deny.
- Progress: the classifier is skipped when there is no new tool call since its last verdict. No verdict means not looping.

 --body 'A pass in a busy project can need more than the cap: it runs the whole test suite more than once, and other builds share the machine. When the cap ends such a pass, its work is half done, and the next pass pays again for reading and writing the same files.

If the verdict is "not looping", the session goes on for another stretch as long as the cap. A session with no verdict, or with a "looping" verdict, ends at the cap as before. - Pass C "is quiet": it made no tool call since the start, so there is no verdict.

2. A has a "not looping" verdict, so it gets stretch 2. The log shows an extend line with the reason.
3. B was already cancelled at 300 s by its looping verdict, so nothing is left to extend.
4. C has no verdict, so the cap ends it.
5. At 1800 s, A reaches its third stretch. The session ends there even with a "not looping" verdict.

A          start....verdict:ok..cap->extend..cap->extend..ceiling X
B          start....verdict:loop X
C          start...................cap X

ok = "not looping"   loop = "looping"   X = session ends   extend = another stretch of the cap
